abstract: The discovery of geroprotectors, defined as interventions that slow aging-related deterioration and preserve function, remains constrained by reliance on lifespan studies. Lifespan studies take years, are costly and resource intensive, and return a whole-organism endpoint dominated in mice by neoplastic death. These studies cannot be readily scaled and do not specify which tissue(s) are protected by geroprotectors. Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cells provide a scalable alternative that enables defined lineages and genetically diverse donors to be studied in parallel. However, reprogramming resets epigenetic age, and whether iPSC-derived cells can report responses relevant to aging has remained unclear. Here, we evaluated eight candidate geroprotectors in iPSC-derived neurons using multiple classes of aging-associated transcriptomic readouts. Aging-associated pathways, including mTORC1 and MEK-ERK signaling, were intact and pharmacologically tunable in these cells. Genetic background accounted for most transcriptional variance, with compound responses differing in magnitude and reproducibility between donors. PI-103 suppressed the mTORC1 signature and increased DCX and BDNF expression, while also inducing genes associated with older age in two independent human excitatory-neuron references. These findings indicate that distinct aging measures capture different dimensions of drug response and that no single readout is sufficient to define geroprotection in our model. Together, these results support iPSC-derived cells as a scalable screening tool for candidate geroprotectors, enabled by the transcriptional aging readouts now available, with the potential to resolve tissue- and donor-dependent responses as additional lineages and donors are incorporated.
